title: A Letter to the South
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass two
content:
The letter from the South Pole arrived folded inside a cloth packet stained with travel salt.

Katara recognized the stitching before she read a word.

"My aunt made this," she said.

Her fingers paused over the blue thread along the seam. It was the kind of pause that told me the letter mattered before I knew what it contained.

Aang stood by the window with Appa's feed schedule in his hand. Toph had one foot against the floor, listening to the delivery cart pull away.

I stayed at the table and let Katara open it herself.

She read the first page quickly. On the second, her expression changed.

"Someone is sick?" Aang asked.

"Not exactly."

She finished reading.

"The southern clinic is running low on certain herbs. The supply ships have been delayed. There are more patients than beds after the ice-breakup storms, and the healers want me to come help organize a new treatment room."

Aang put down the schedule.

"When do they need you?"

"Now."

Toph leaned back in her chair.

"Well, that's a terrible invitation."

Katara folded the letter along its old creases.

"It's home."

Nobody argued with that.

The harder part came later.

We had been planning to attend the Riverstone bridge inspection together, the first one after the repairs. Katara was supposed to lead the clinic volunteers at the reopened crossing. Aang had promised to speak to the council. Toph had already threatened the mortar with consequences.

And I had planned a whole evening with Katara.

I looked at the calendar we'd spent so much time making.

"How soon can you leave?" I asked.

She looked at me with an expression I couldn't read.

"Tomorrow. Perhaps tonight if Appa is ready."

I nodded.

"Then we need to find someone who can cover the clinic."

"Jasper."

I looked up.

"You're not angry?"

"About the letter?"

"About leaving."

"Why would I be angry that people you love need you?"

She set the letter on the table.

"Because we've barely finished deciding how to make time for each other. Because I've had to leave before. Because you have other relationships and I know you don't need me here every night."

The words came out in a rush. Then she looked embarrassed by how much she'd revealed.

I went around the table and stood where she could see me.

"I don't need you here every night to care about you," I said. "I want you to have a home you can leave and return to. I also want you to tell me when you're scared I'll stop waiting. Those are different conversations."

Toph nodded once.

"Finally, somebody said it."

Aang rubbed the back of his neck.

"I think I've been afraid of that too," he admitted.

Katara looked at him.

"Afraid of what?"

"That every time duty takes us in different directions, we come back a little less like we were."

Toph made a face.

"Of course we do. That's the point of living."

We all looked at her.

She lifted her chin.

"What? You want a relationship with people who never change? Try dating statues."

I laughed, startled. Katara's mouth twitched.

Toph leaned forward.

"You'll go South. We'll miss you. You'll come back. We'll talk about what happened, and maybe something will be different. That's not a tragedy. It's just a Wednesday with a lot of snow."

Katara crossed the room and hugged her so suddenly that Toph made an outraged noise.

"Stop making me look emotionally available!"

"Too late," I said.

Aang joined them. I stayed back until Katara reached for me.

We spent the afternoon planning what needed planning. Aang arranged travel with Appa. I spoke to the clinic volunteers about interim shifts. Toph checked the footbridge one more time so the committee could begin its work without Katara having to carry the entire project from another continent.

The first proposed supply list came back from the Southern clinic with half its entries crossed out.

Katara stared at it. "They don't need more blankets. They need clean treatment space, fish oil and the right herbs. Sending the wrong things just fills the room they are trying to repair."

Aang had already drawn a route for Appa. "I could carry another load."

"You can carry what the clinic coordinator actually requests," Katara said. "Not whatever makes us feel useful."

Toph tapped the floor beside the table. "And don't forget the platform. Their last letter said the steps were iced over."

"I remember," Katara said. "They have a plan to clear them. I want to know if the path is wide enough for the equipment."

I checked the list of Lanternweald garden stores. Tideglass had some useful plants, but the coastal beds were not an endless apothecary and not a substitute for medicine selected by healers familiar with the South. I left the quantities blank until the clinic could confirm what it would accept.

Aang crossed out his extra cargo run. "Okay. No heroic surprise shipment."

"You're learning," Toph said.

He gave her a wounded look. "I thought this was about helping."

"It is," Katara said. "That's why we're asking."

When the others went out to check Appa's harness, Katara leaned against the table. The salt-stained packet from home rested beneath her hand.

"I'm afraid I'll get there and find out how much I missed," she admitted.

I reached for her fingers and let her decide whether to hold them. She did.

"Then you'll tell me what you want to share," I said.

She drew me closer by the front of my shirt. Her kiss was brief and hungry enough to interrupt the worry for a moment, not erase it.

Outside, Toph called that somebody had put the harness buckle on backwards. Katara laughed against my cheek.

"We should rescue him," I said.

"No," she murmured. "Let's give him a minute to solve his own problem."

The travel packet stayed on the kitchen table.

I touched it once, feeling the uneven seam beneath my fingers. Katara watched me.

"What?" she asked.

"Your aunt's stitching is crooked."

"She was repairing three fishing nets and a sleeping mat when she made that."

"Then I retract the criticism."

"Wise."

She smiled, but her eyes were wet.

Before dinner, Katara asked to speak to the clinic's coordinator through the agreed message route. She wanted to know what the staff needed, not just what the letter had frightened her into imagining.

The answer came back with a practical list. Two local healers were already managing the treatment room. They wanted Katara to demonstrate a few procedures and help revise a supply ledger, then leave them able to do the work without her. The visit was important, but she wasn't being summoned to save people who lacked their own judgment.

"That is better news than I expected," she said.

Aang offered to arrange transport but waited for her decision. Toph asked how long Appa would need to rest between the outward and return journeys. Nobody made the itinerary into a competition over who was most helpful.

I looked at our calendar. "Would you like a quiet hour with me before you go?"

Katara glanced at the departure time. "Half an hour. And I want a little time alone to pack the medical notes."

"All right."

Aang asked whether she'd like company on the first leg. She did. Toph decided to stay and check the bridge inspection rather than come along because she hated missing work she'd actually promised to do. We each had somewhere to be and someone who might miss us.

I was still frightened that the house would feel different when Katara came back. Our relationship was openly polyamorous by choice, and we'd made that agreement because nobody was meant to be trapped in one version of the household. Knowing it didn't remove the ache. It just kept me from treating her trip as disloyalty.

Katara took my hand for a moment. "You don't have to be cheerful about this."

"I know."

"Good. I wasn't planning to be."

Then she went to pack the notes, and we kept our small piece of time before the evening's departure.

We ate dinner early because Aang wanted to leave before the weather changed. Toph told terrible jokes about snow. Katara pretended not to enjoy them. I packed an extra scarf into her bag and tucked a small folded note beside the medical supplies.

She found it before we reached the courtyard.

READ THIS WHEN SOMEONE TELLS YOU THAT YOU HAVE TO BE EVERYWHERE AT ONCE.

She unfolded it.

YOU ARE ALLOWED TO BE ONE PERSON IN ONE PLACE. WE CAN DO OUR PART HERE.

Katara pressed her lips together.

"You'll make me cry before I board."

"Then I'll claim it's the wind."

"Awful excuse."

"Very professional."

She kissed me beside the open door. The air was cold, and she tasted faintly of mint tea. Her hands settled at my waist, warm through the fabric. I felt how much I wanted to ask her to stay, and how relieved I was that wanting did not have to become a demand.

When she drew back, Aang was checking Appa's saddle.

Toph stood beside him, listening to the sky.

"Weather's coming," she said.

"Can you feel the clouds?" I asked.

"No. But Twinkle Toes is making that face."

Aang laughed.

Katara climbed onto Appa and turned to look down at us.

"I'll write."

"Don't promise a schedule you can't keep," I said.

She smiled.

"I'll write when I can."

"Good."

They rose into the evening, a broad shadow moving across the rooftops. Toph stayed beside me until Appa disappeared beyond the hills.

"You're quiet," she said.

"Missing her already."

"Yeah."

She took my hand.

We stood there until the cold reached our fingers.

Over the next few days, the house changed shape without her. Aang returned after bringing Katara safely to the South, and the three of us learned where she had quietly handled small things we hadn't noticed. The clinic inventory was missing a signature. The pantry needed water. Someone had to mend the curtain that kept blowing over the stove.

We did those things.

When a letter finally arrived, it carried two pages of Katara's handwriting and a tiny sketch of the treatment room she'd helped repair. The roof had stopped leaking. The beds were full. She was exhausted and happy to have something useful to do.

At the bottom, she had written:

I MISS YOU. ALL OF YOU. PLEASE DO NOT TURN THE HOUSE INTO A DISASTER WHILE I'M GONE.

Toph snorted.

"Too late."

Aang looked at the pile of laundry he'd promised to fold.

I folded the letter and set it on the table beside four bowls.

One of them was empty.

It did not feel like a threat.

It felt like a place waiting to be used whenever the person who belonged there chose to return.
